subject: physics

items.q: A ball of mass 500 g is moving at a speed of 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
items.why: The number in the question is the one that feels 'given', and the unit written next to it is read over rather than checked. The equation requires the mass in kilograms. Divide a mass in grams by 1000 before substituting: 500 g = 0.5 kg.

items.q: A toy car of mass 0.8 kg is moving at a speed of 5 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
items.misconception: 2 J
items.why: The equation is remembered as the spoken phrase 'half m v', and the small index is lost when it is written out from memory under time pressure. The equation is kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2. Square the speed first and write the squared value down (5^2 = 25) before multiplying by the mass and by 0.5.

items.q: A van doubles its speed. Its mass does not change. What happens to its kinetic energy?
items.correct: it becomes four times as large as before
items.misconception: it becomes eight times as big as before
items.why: Most GCSE relationships met before this point are directly proportional, so doubling one quantity is expected to double the other. Only speed is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2, so a factor of 2 on the speed becomes a factor of 2^2 = 4 on the energy. Test it with numbers: 0.5 x 60 x 4^2 = 480 J, but 0.5 x 60 x 8^2 = 1920 J.
items.random_wrong: it becomes twice as large as before

items.q: Which of these is the equation E_k = 1/2 m v^2 written out in words?
items.misconception: kinetic energy = 0.5 × (mass)^2 × (speed)
items.why: The equation is recalled as 'a half, a mass, a speed and a square', and the square is attached to whichever symbol is written first. Only the speed is squared. Writing the equation in words as kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2 keeps the bracket around the right quantity.
items.random_wrong: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed

items.q: A kinetic energy calculation uses a mass in kilograms and a speed in metres per second. The answer is in which unit?
items.misconception: newtons, N
items.why: Newtons and watts are the units met alongside energy in mechanics, and unit symbols are memorised as a set rather than paired with their quantities. Every energy store in this section is measured in joules, J. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power.
items.random_wrong: watts, W

items.q: A student puts the mass of a 250 g ball straight into E_k = 1/2 m v^2 as 250. Why is the answer wrong?
items.correct: the mass has to be in kilograms, so m should be 0.25
items.misconception: the speed should have been squared before the mass
items.why: The equation is remembered as the spoken phrase 'half m v', and the small index is lost when it is written out from memory under time pressure. The equation is kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2. Square the speed first and write the squared value down (5^2 = 25) before multiplying by the mass and by 0.5.
items.random_wrong: the mass has to be in newtons, so m should be 2.5

items.q: A car's speed is given as 72 km/h. What must be done before using E_k = 1/2 m v^2?
items.correct: convert the speed to metres per second
items.misconception: convert the speed into kilometres per minute
items.why: Everyday speeds are quoted in km/h or mph, so those units feel like the natural ones for a speed. In this equation the speed must be in metres per second, m/s, because that is the only speed unit that gives an energy in joules.
items.random_wrong: use 72 as the speed and convert the answer

items.q: Which pair of quantities is needed to calculate the kinetic energy of a moving object?
items.correct: the mass and the speed of the object
items.misconception: the force applied and the speed reached
items.why: Work done is calculated from force and distance, and that equation is met close to this one, so its quantities are borrowed. Kinetic energy is worked out from mass and speed alone. Force and distance give the work done, which is a different calculation.
items.random_wrong: the weight and the speed of the object

items.q: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched, within its limit of proportionality, so that its extension is 0.1 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?
items.why: The extension is a small decimal, and squaring a decimal feels wrong because the answer gets smaller, so the step is skipped. The equation is elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2. Square the extension first: 0.1^2 = 0.01.

items.q: A spring with a spring constant of 400 N/m is stretched by an extension of 5 cm, staying within its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
items.misconception: 1 J
items.why: The 0.5 looks like a small tidying-up number rather than part of the physics, so it is dropped when the equation is rewritten quickly. Both E_k = 1/2 m v^2 and E_e = 1/2 k e^2 begin with a factor of 0.5, and leaving it out doubles every answer.

items.q: The energy stored in a stretched spring is E_e = 1/2 k e^2. What do the symbols k and e stand for?
items.correct: the spring constant and the extension of the spring
items.misconception: the spring constant and the energy of the spring
items.why: The subscript in Ee and the symbol e look alike, so the two are read as the same thing. Ee is the elastic potential energy and e is the extension. The equation therefore has energy on one side and extension, squared, on the other.
items.random_wrong: the spring constant and the force applied to it

items.q: A spring is stretched within its limit of proportionality. The elastic potential energy stored in it is measured in which unit?
items.misconception: newtons, N
items.why: Newtons and watts are the units met alongside energy in mechanics, and unit symbols are memorised as a set rather than paired with their quantities. Every energy store in this section is measured in joules, J. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power.
items.random_wrong: watts, W

items.q: In the equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2, the spring constant k is measured in which unit?
items.misconception: newtons times metres, N m
items.why: Several similar-looking compound units appear in this part of the course, and they are stored as a list of symbols rather than attached to their quantities. The spring constant is the force needed per metre of extension, so it is newtons per metre, N/m. N/kg belongs to gravitational field strength, and N m is a unit of energy.
items.random_wrong: newtons per kilogram, N/kg

items.q: A spring of unstretched length 0.20 m is stretched to a length of 0.26 m. Which length is the extension e used in E_e = 1/2 k e^2?
items.correct: the increase in length, in metres
items.misconception: the whole stretched length, in metres
items.why: The stretched length is the number the ruler shows at the end of the experiment, so it is read as 'the length of the spring' without subtracting. The extension is the increase in length: stretched length minus original length. It is zero for an unstretched spring, which the total length never is.
items.random_wrong: the length before stretching, in metres

items.q: A spring is stretched so far that its limit of proportionality has been exceeded. What does this mean for E_e = 1/2 k e^2?
items.correct: the equation can no longer be used to find the energy
items.misconception: the equation still works if e is measured again
items.why: The equation is learned as a formula that works for springs, and the bracketed condition in the specification is read as a side note rather than a restriction. The specification states the equation assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. Beyond that limit, extension is no longer proportional to force and the equation no longer gives the energy stored.
items.random_wrong: the spring constant doubles from that point on

items.q: Which two quantities must be known to calculate the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring?
items.correct: the spring constant and the extension
items.misconception: the spring constant and the force used
items.why: The other two energy equations in this section both contain a mass, so a mass is expected here too. E_e = 1/2 k e^2 contains no mass and no force: only the spring constant, in N/m, and the extension, in m.
items.random_wrong: the mass of the spring and its extension

items.q: A book of mass 800 g is lifted through a height of 1.5 m. The gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. How much gravitational potential energy does the book gain?
items.why: The conversion is an extra step that is easily skipped when the arithmetic itself looks straightforward. The mass in E_p = m g h must be in kilograms. Convert first: 800 g = 0.8 kg.
items.random_wrong: 6 J

items.q: A box is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp and ends up 2.0 m above the ground. Which value is used as h in E_p = m g h?
items.correct: 2.0 m, the vertical height risen above the ground
items.misconception: 5.0 m, the distance moved along the ramp surface
items.why: The 5.0 m is the distance the box actually travelled, so it feels like the quantity that describes the movement. In E_p = m g h, h is the vertical height above the starting level. The path taken does not change the gravitational potential energy gained.
items.random_wrong: 3.0 m, the difference in the two distances

items.q: Which of these is g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height written in symbols, with the correct unit?
items.correct: E_p = m g h, giving E_p in joules
items.misconception: E_p = 1/2 m g h, giving E_p in joules
items.why: The other two energy equations in this section both start with 0.5, so the half is carried across as though every energy equation had one. g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height. There is no factor of 0.5: the half appears only where a quantity is squared.
items.random_wrong: E_p = m g h, giving E_p in watts

items.q: In E_p = m g h, what is g and where does its value come from?
items.correct: field strength in N/kg, given in the question
items.misconception: field strength in N/kg, which must be recalled
items.why: Two different values appear in textbooks and past papers, so students assume recall is being tested. The specification says that in any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength will be given. Read the value from the question and use it as printed.
items.random_wrong: field strength in N, given in the exam question

items.q: A ball has a mass of 0.25 kg. What is substituted for m?
items.misconception: You convert the mass into a weight in newtons first, or you describe the mass in grams as a weight.
items.why: In everyday speech 'weight' is used for what a balance measures, so mass and weight are treated as the same quantity with a choice of units. Mass is measured in kilograms and is what m stands for in all three equations. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for m.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A trolley of mass 2 kg moves at 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
items.misconception: You work out 0.5 x 5^2 = 12.5 J, leaving the mass out altogether.
items.why: The squaring of the speed takes all the attention, and the mass is the quantity most easily forgotten once the square has been dealt with. Three numbers are multiplied together in E_k = 1/2 m v^2: 0.5, the mass and the squared speed. Check that all three appear in your working.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spring of spring constant 400 N/m has an extension of 5 cm. Find the energy stored.
items.misconception: You substitute 5 for the extension and obtain 5000 J.
items.why: Extensions are measured with a centimetre ruler, so the centimetre reading is the number in front of the student when the equation is written. The extension must be in metres before it is squared. Divide a centimetre value by 100: 5 cm = 0.05 m. Squaring magnifies the error, so an unconverted value is out by a factor of 10 000.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A book of mass 0.8 kg is lifted 1.5 m. g = 10 N/kg. Find the g.p.e. gained.
items.misconception: You work out 0.8 x 1.5 = 1.2 J, leaving the gravitational field strength out.
items.why: Mass and height are the two quantities that describe the object and the lift, so g feels like a constant that is quoted rather than used. Three quantities are multiplied in E_p = m g h. The value of g is given in the question precisely because it must be substituted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A van doubles its speed while its mass stays the same. What happens to its kinetic energy?
items.correct: It becomes four times as large.
items.misconception: You say it is unchanged, because the mass of the van has not changed.
items.why: Mass is the quantity that feels permanent and object-like, so it is treated as the thing that fixes the energy an object has. Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, and on the square of the speed. A stationary van has no kinetic energy at all, whatever its mass.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In E_e = 1/2 k e^2, what does e stand for?
items.correct: The extension of the spring, in metres.
items.misconception: You read e as the effort, or force, applied to the spring.
items.why: Force is what causes the stretch, so it is the quantity students expect an equation about stretching to contain. The force does not appear in this equation. Its effect is already contained in the extension e and the spring constant k.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the unit of gravitational field strength g?
items.misconception: You give newtons, N, because you think g is the force of gravity itself.
items.why: The phrase 'the pull of gravity' is used for both the field strength and the weight, so the two quantities merge. Gravitational field strength is the force acting on each kilogram, so it is newtons per kilogram, N/kg. The force itself, the weight, is in newtons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m has an extension of 0.1 m. Find the energy stored.
items.misconception: You square the spring constant instead of the extension, working out 0.5 x 200^2 x 0.1 = 2000 J.
items.why: The extension is a small decimal that gets smaller when squared, which feels wrong, so the square is moved onto the larger, more equation-looking number. In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the index belongs to the extension only. Writing the equation in words as elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2 keeps the bracket in the right place.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.1.2 Changes in energy
